newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile forestry firms blast U.S. court ruling.
newsitem.headline: Chile forestry firms blast U.S. court ruling.

text.p: Chilean forestry companies slammed a U.S. court ruling on Friday banning new import permits for logs and wood chips from Chile and two other countries, saying the order was a new form of protectionism.
"We consider that the measure is tremendously serious," Fernando Leniz, president of forestry lobby group Corporacion Chilena de la Madera (Corma), told a news conference.
"It is an extremely serious precedent for the obstruction of international trade."
A San Francisco federal court upheld mid-June appeals by four U.S. environmental groups against the granting of new permits to import pine logs and wood chips from Chile, New Zealand and Russia.

The court banned the Agriculture Department from issuing the new permits on the grounds that products from these three countries have not been proved to be free of diseases which could infect North American trees.
The row over the forestry imports is the second trade dispute in recent months between Chile and the United States.
Chile is defending its salmon raisers against allegations from U.S. producers of dumping and illegal subsidies in a dispute being analyzed at the U.S. Trade Department.
Last year, Chile exported pine logs worth $12 million to the United States -- a small part of the forestry industry's total exports which were worth over $1.8 billion in 1996.
Chilean companies have written to the Agriculture Department to complain about the ruling, said Leniz.
The four Chilean firms who export logs and chips to the United States already have permits for this year, so the order will only have an impact in 1998, he said.
"This (U.S.) agency will be forbidden from issuing new permits in 1998," said Leniz.
Company officials blasted the ruling as a "new form of protectionism" and said this type of order could affect other products exported to the United States.
Chile's forestry industry has boomed in the last 20 years with thousands of hectares of fast-growing pine and eucalyptus plantations blanketing hills in the country's cool south.
Some species, including North American pine, grow faster in Chile than in their native territory.
